speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Act was last amended in 2011 and a review is, therefore, timely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In preparing for this Bill, we consulted many stakeholders, including social service agencies, volunteers and professionals, and I met some of them in May this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They gave strong support for the proposed changes and also provided valuable feedback.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The concerns and suggestions they have raised helped us to make many refinements to the Bill that Members see now before you.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are set out in section 3A of the existing Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, parents have the primary responsibility for the care and welfare of their child; and second, in administering or applying the Act, the welfare and best interests of the child must be the first and paramount consideration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Section 28 of the existing Act also sets out the considerations that the Youth Court must take into account when it hears cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under clause 24 of the Bill before Members, we propose to widen this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Youth Court should not only aim to facilitate the protection and rehabilitation of the child but also facilitate his reintegration with his family and with society; and second, the Youth Court should have regard to the needs of and risks faced by the child and prevent any further ill-treatment or offending.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We do this to ensure better outcomes for children and break the cycles of abuse, neglect and offending.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you look at the infographic that we have just distributed, you will see four pockets of amendments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will take you through the Bill in the course of its Second Reading and you can follow accordingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we will cover provisions that safeguard the interests of abused or neglected children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, taking action and intervening for children who are abused or neglected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The second group of amendments relate to improving the rehabilitation and reintegration of youths with offending behaviour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The third relates to guiding families in their parenting, with support from the community; and most people would refer to this as the beyond parental control regime (BPC).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Lastly, strengthening partnerships with the community to care for vulnerable children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, the Act allows us to intervene to protect children below 16 years of age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is in line with the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of the Child, to which Singapore is a signatory.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under the Act today, we can intervene to provide care and protection to a child in a range of situations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One of these is if "there is such a serious and persistent conflict within the family that relationships are seriously disrupted and the child suffers emotional injury".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, the term "emotional injury" is not defined, giving rise to confusion about whether we can intervene.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) has also encountered other situations where a child's emotional well-being has been severely affected and help should be rendered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Emotional harm which causes serious impairment to the child may not always be as readily or immediately observable as physical injuries, such as bruises or burns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The clause also provides a non-exhaustive list of circumstances in which a child is deemed to be in need of care and protection because of emotional or psychological abuse by parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are based on established child protection guidelines, such as those from the American Professional Society on the Abuse of Children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By sharpening the meaning of emotional or psychological abuse, the amendments give better guidance to all stakeholders – MSF, social service agencies and the Court – on when we should intervene and when we need not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Take the example of Valerie, not her real name.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Valerie's mother would deliberately isolate her at home or confine her to her room to minimise her interactions with other people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She frequently told Valerie that she was dirty, smelly and unclean and refused to hold her "unclean" hands.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She also frequently blamed Valerie for anything and everything that went wrong.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When a relative who took care of Valerie fell ill, the mother would call Valerie a jinx.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Whenever her father tried to protect or side with her, the mother would threaten to commit suicide.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Valerie was very much affected by the emotional abuse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She fears and, not unexpectedly, bears hatred towards her mother.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Her anger, coupled with anxiety, has manifested as aggressive and rough play in school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is a 10-year-old girl who needs help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to see past her behaviour and recognise the emotional harm that is within.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I highlight Valerie's case to show that emotional or psychological abuse and its impact may not be as readily observable as physical abuse and injury, but the harm to a child is no less significant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The new amendments make clear that cases like Valerie's fall within the scope of CYPA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where children have to be removed from their families due to safety concerns, it can be unsettling for them to be placed in an unfamiliar environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Their anxiety may be compounded if there are changes from their usual routine.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or the children may feel abnormal or inferior to their school mates, if placed in situations that remind them of their incomplete families and disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The persons who are entrusted with the care of such children, such as foster parents or staff of children's homes, handle a range of matters related to the child's welfare and development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This can range from day-to-day care matters, such as personal grooming, dietary arrangements and health vaccinations, to more substantial matters, such as overseas travel, choice of school, surgery and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Particularly, where the matters are more sensitive or significant, the caregivers would wish to respect the views of the child's parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But getting parental consent can sometimes be challenging because these are the very parents from whom the children have had to be removed for safety reasons in the very first place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some will not cooperate and make things difficult for the foster parent or the children's home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As a result, the development and emotional well-being of the children who have been removed for safety reasons can be further affected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill enables MSF and designated caregivers to provide smooth and stable out-of-home care arrangements for such children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: More substantive decisions for the children, such as overseas travel, can be made only if MSF establishes that the parents cannot be contacted despite reasonable efforts, or are otherwise incapable or unwilling to decide.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Of the children who are in out-of-home care, MSF has handled cases where, despite the best efforts of professionals and the community, it is not possible nor in the interest of the child to be reunified with his parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Take, for example, five-year-old Joshua, again not his real name.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Joshua was referred to MSF for possible neglect by his mother.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He has a developmental disorder and requires extra care to meet his developmental milestones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: His mother was diagnosed with a mental health condition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF placed Joshua with foster parents, who were harassed by Joshua's mother because of her delusional belief that they were ill-treating him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The mother was also unable to consistently adhere with her treatment plans and her mental health condition was assessed to be long-term.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Given the condition of Joshua's mother and her poor response to medical treatment, it would not be in Joshua's best interests to be reunified with her.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She would not be able to adequately care for Joshua, especially with his special needs and young age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Other scenarios where reunification is not in the interests of the child are where the parent had severely ill-treated or allowed other persons to severely ill-treat the child or another child under his care and custody; the parent had been convicted of causing or trying to cause death to a child in his care and custody, or to the other parent of the child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In these scenarios and for cases like Joshua's, the children are likely to spend many years and perhaps even the majority of their childhood in out-of-home care despite best efforts at reunification.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But sensitive decisions that are neither day-to-day in nature nor ordinarily made in the care of a child, can only be made with parental consent or the Court's authorisation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ben is today 13 years old, has multiple conditions that require frequent medical appointments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ben's mother has been unwilling to care for him since he was born.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Once, Ben was admitted to the hospital for a persistently high fever.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Doctors recommended surgery to prevent further medical complications but Ben's mother was unwilling to provide consent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF had to apply to the Court for orders to allow Ben to undergo the necessary surgery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At this point, I wish to assure Members that the ECPO does not sever the legal ties between parent and child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Parents who disagree with any decision made by MSF or designated caregivers can bring the matter to Court for determination.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And even after an ECPO is made, parents may apply to vary or revoke the order, if there has been a material change in circumstances from the time when the ECPO was made.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This requires the parents to demonstrate significant and sustained changes in addressing the safety concerns that have hitherto hindered family reunification and the child must be assessed to be ready for contact with the family and eventual reunification.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are among some of the biggest-hearted people in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Children grow up best in a supportive family environment, especially if they have been abused or neglected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, MSF's preference is to place such children in foster families, rather than in residential facilities, such as children's homes, if it can be helped.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These foster families have opened their hearts and their homes to provide their foster children with the opportunity to grow up with a positive experience of family life, an opportunity that many of us take for granted but which vulnerable children may not have.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If Members could look at the infographic handed out to Members earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These relate to the rehabilitation of children and young persons with offending behaviour whom I will subsequently refer to as youths or youth offenders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are many reasons why youths commit offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sometimes, it is because of challenging family circumstances, negative influences or the absence of family support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They need handholding and good role models so that they can pick themselves up and make responsible decisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We seek to make a few major changes in this area.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we want to cover older youths under the youth justice framework, instead of treating them as adult offenders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we need to take steps to enhance the safety of all youths who are housed in MSF's Youth Homes as well as the staff working in our Homes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, we seek to treat youth offenders' criminal records as spent after they have completed their Youth Court orders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, the Youth Court hears cases against youth offenders who are below 16 years of age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Young people who are 16 and above who commit offences are tried as adults in the State Courts or the Community Court, unless they are diverted away from the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But studies have shown that these young persons may still not have the full cognitive maturity of adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: An inter-agency committee chaired by the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) to review the youth justice system had also recommended allowing them to benefit from a wider range of sentencing options.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will be the default mode for most youth offenders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we need to retain an avenue for exceptions, such as for youth offenders who are 16 and above but below 18 years, who commit serious offences, such as gang or drug-related activities or unlicensed moneylending, or who are repeat offenders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Clause 55 of the Bill inserts a new Second Schedule to the Act which spells out the full list of serious offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When the offender has committed such a serious offence or if he is not a first-time offender, clause 27 gives the Public Prosecutor the discretion to charge the offender in either the Youth Court or a Court of appropriate jurisdiction, such as the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is intended as a deterrent that we are not soft on crimes, especially those of a serious nature, and that there are times where firmer punishment of the offender is warranted, in spite of his youth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Clause 27 also allows the Youth Court to decide, on its own motion, that another Court of appropriate jurisdiction is to try the case and mete out the appropriate sentencing for these offenders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This addresses the current gap where some youth offenders reject probation in favour of a shorter imprisonment term in adult prison which works against the Court's and MSF's efforts to help such youth rehabilitate and reintegrate into society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Next, I will turn to the issue of safety and security within MSF's Youth Homes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The guiding philosophy underpinning the work of our two Juvenile Rehabilitation Centres (JRCs) is to rehabilitate, guide and support youth offenders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For that reason, many of the security features present in adult prisons are not found in our JRCs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Yet, at the same time, we need to strike the right balance of measures because, without adequate safety and assurance of security, it will not be possible to provide an environment that is conducive to rehabilitation in our JRCs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even with today's age limit, where youths may be admitted to the JRCs if they are below 16 years of age, there have been incidents where aggressive youths put our youth guidance officers, case workers and other youths at risk of harm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In one case, a 15-year-old youth verbally threatened the staff at the Home every day he was there.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the day of his Court hearing, he pretended to grab the baton of the escorting Police Officer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He then swung his arm towards an MSF officer to intimidate him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Despite being counselled, the youth was recalcitrant and continued to intimidate other youths at the Home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In another case, we had a youth with a history of aggression, including past incidents of punching his schoolmates, getting into fights with strangers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While he was at the Singapore Boys' Home, the youth punched and injured his dormitory mates on various occasions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He also assaulted and injured a few Auxiliary Police Officers and MSF officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are incidents that we need to prevent, and I describe these cases not to adjudicate or assign blame to these young people, but rather that these things can and, indeed, do happen, for whatever reason.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This means recognising that some youths may not be suitable for rehabilitation within a JRC but may instead require a higher level of supervision in a more structured environment, such as Reformative Training.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is also consistent with clause 24, where the Youth Court is to have regard to the needs and risks of children and prevent any further re-offending or ill-treatment of all children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include situations where youths continue to create a disturbance or taunt other residents because such hostile behaviour, if not put to an end, can escalate quickly and compromise safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is the prevailing practice in other jurisdictions, such as in Korea, the United Kingdom (UK) and some States in Australia, for the same purpose of preventing escape, violence, self-injury or other incidents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I wish to assure Members that there will be strict guidelines pertaining to the use of such restraints, and MSF officers must be trained before they are authorised to use the restraints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They will not be used as a punitive measure but to ensure safety and security of both the youth and those around him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our officers are also trained to de-escalate conflicts among residents and prevent incidents of escape, self-injury or harm to others using other safe intervention methods, where possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For youth offenders who have been successfully rehabilitated, we must make sure they have the best shot in life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, often, the label of being an ex-offender tends to stick.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many jobs today require applicants to declare whether they have a criminal record, and some employers hold it against those who do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Doors may remain closed and the sense of rejection can be daunting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These Youth Court orders refer to a JRC order, probation order, community service order, detention order and an order to pay a fine, damages or costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Therefore, after the law is amended, youths who have completed their Youth Court orders can, if asked whether they have ever been convicted or have a criminal record, legitimately declare "No".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sections 27A and 35 of the Act now protect the identity and privacy of a child when he is below 16.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through clause 50, we will widen this to ensure that the identity of a child who is or was in care and custody or the subject of an arrest, investigation, Court order or any proceedings under the CYPA, remains protected for the rest of his life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, if the individual were to commit more offences when he is older after he turns 18, the protection of identity will not apply to these subsequent offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These amendments signal our commitment to better protect and support our youths in their journey to reintegrate with family and society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have met many former young offenders who have successfully turned their lives around while under our care and supervision.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Take, for example, Jasper Yap, a former resident of the Singapore Boys' Home, whom I consulted when I was gathering feedback on this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Jasper discovered he was capable of studying and doing well when he scored his first A during his stay at the Singapore Boys' Home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He is now an entrepreneur and currently serving National Service.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Jasper is also a member of the Youth Advisory Group advising MSF, the Ministry of Home Affairs and other Ministries on youth policy work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He shares his rehabilitation journey with the youths in the Singapore Boys' Home and teaches them ways to kick their bad habits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Like Jasper, we want to help our youths to have good role models and opportunities to succeed in life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These seek to reform the area of practice currently known as Beyond Parental Control (BPC).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, parents can apply to the Youth Court to seek help for children who are labelled as BPC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The children may display difficult behaviour, such as running away or being in the wrong company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Court may place the BPC children under the supervision of an appointed person, or in a residential setting, such as a children's home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The term BPC blames the child and holds him solely responsible for his behaviour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is not just a mere change of name.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Court may allow the parents to first file an FGO application and then have the family complete the family programme later if, for example, the child refuses to attend the family programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Court can also order parents to attend mediation, counselling, psychotherapy or programmes before, during or after FGO applications are heard.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is in contrast to the existing framework where the Court can give such orders to the parents only after a BPC order has been made for the child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I spoke earlier that we are expanding coverage of the Act to persons aged below 18 if they face abuse or neglect or have committed offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is because older youths are more likely to resent or resist participating in programmes and resent being brought to Court by their parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are, therefore, keeping the age limit at below 16 so as not to worsen family relationships that may already be strained.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We do this after taking significant advice from professionals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will now talk about the last bucket of amendments which will strengthen partnerships with the community to care for vulnerable children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Child protection work is currently done by MSF's Child Protective Service (CPS) and they partner our social service agencies who also play an important role.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, social service agencies, such as Montfort Care and Fei Yue Community Services, run Child Protection Specialist Centres (CPSCs), as well as Family Service Centres (FSCs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But child protection work also involves many dedicated, trained volunteers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is especially important if we want to keep families intact and ensure the safety of children within the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Clause 3 allows MSF to appoint members of the public to carry out specified duties under the Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These individuals are known as Volunteer Welfare Officers in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, in child abuse cases, volunteer welfare officers can conduct visits to the child's home to monitor his well-being and safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These volunteers will receive training and they may act only under MSF's instruction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Clause 7 also allows MSF to share information relating to a child with community partners, such as the Child Protection Specialist Centres and children's homes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The purpose is to enable our partners to intervene quickly to protect vulnerable children from harm and work with families to pre-emptively resolve issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These persons would include volunteer welfare officers and foster parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The participation of volunteers in complementing MSF's statutory work of protection and rehabilitation is not new.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, volunteers assist MSF's Probation Officers by befriending, guiding and supervising probationers, and volunteers from the Singapore Boys' Home and Girls' Home support rehabilitation and reintegration, such as by befriending youths and providing tuition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Volunteers help provide transport to children under the supervision of MSF's Child Protective Service, such as to and from their residence to medical appointments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The overwhelming majority of families do their best to care for, protect and raise their children well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, when it comes to the small number of families who require help to fulfil basic responsibilities to their children, the proposals in this Bill are vitally important and may, in some cases, literally be a lifesaver.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It also supports children who have committed offences, those who have been abused or neglected by their parents or caregivers, and those whose parents are seeking the Court's guidance because of their children's behaviour.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The importance of this Act cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Children who go through a traumatic experience or have challenges when they are young are more likely to have issues when they are older.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The research done by Rasmus Birn, Barbara Roeburn and Seth Pollak in 2017 explained that individuals who have experienced chronic and high levels of stress during their childhoods are at increased risk for a wide range of behavioural problems, yet the neurobiological mechanisms underlying this association are poorly understood.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They measured the life circumstances of a community sample of school-age children and then followed these children for a decade and found that those who had experienced extreme stress as children were hampered in their ability to make good decisions as adults.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Simply put, childhood trauma, due to circumstances like neglect or exposure to violence, created young adults fundamentally unable to correctly consider risk and make healthy life decisions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In fact, no threat of punishment was likely to be effective in changing this deficit.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon, in his keynote address at the Conference on At-Risk Youths in 2015, aptly said: "In general, it can be said that the more a child is exposed to adverse circumstances at an early age, the more disadvantaged will that child be." Indeed, it has been suggested that the strongest predictors of whether a child will eventually turn to crime are likely to be in such things as poor parental supervision, parental conflict, disrupted families and, most notably, having parents with a criminal or anti-social background.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is, therefore, a matter of some importance that we keep an eye on the state of our families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Many studies have shown that whenever children undergo traumatic experiences or challenges when they are younger, it will have a profound impact on their lives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One such study conducted in 2017 stated that childhood trauma, possibly due to the child being abandoned or exposed to violence, will create youths and adults who are unable to assess risks and make healthy and correct decisions in life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is clear that traumatic experiences will affect the trajectory or direction in the life of a child or a youth.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, this CYPA Bill is an important piece of legislation that protects children and young persons from danger and facilitates rehabilitation, if required, as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a community, we must also continue to support and guide parents, especially those who are facing challenges because they may have had traumatic or bad experiences themselves when they were young.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Perhaps the support and assistance for parents who face issues with their children should be enhanced so that they can understand the process that they are undergoing and be equipped with the skills to educate their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As much as possible, we would like the family to stay intact and live harmoniously, but the most important thing to do is to protect children from precarious or hazardous situations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Childhood and youth are points in life when one is supposed to be the most carefree and protected.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, this experience may not be true for some children or young people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to help those undergoing challenging periods as much as we can.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The underlying principle of any regulation in this respect must be that the welfare and best interests of the children and young person will be the paramount consideration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that the work done by all the officers and caregivers in this sector is not easy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I, therefore, acknowledge the need to review and make amendments to this Act over time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I support the amendments but have a few matters which I wish to seek clarification on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Those who are under 18 are still young, generally less mature cognitively and are still, therefore, vulnerable to abuse and neglect.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They should also be given the necessary attention and appropriate rehabilitative support when they offend.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, when we deal with young offenders, a wider age range of young people may be placed within the same residential facility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The needs and risks of a small child and a physically larger youth would differ and present different challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have already received some anecdotal feedback about the instances of bullying in some of the residential homes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Typically, it happens when one resident or a group of them feel that they have more control and power over another.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Further, will it be more difficult to coordinate targeted programmes or support for rehabilitation when you have a wider age group in the residential homes?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The increase of the age limit will not only increase the numbers but, as alluded to above, the different group of young people will have a new profile with differing needs and risks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What is the plan to strengthen the ability of the Ministry and the social service agencies to operationalise the amendments?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am a little bothered by the possible scenarios and the impact such actions would have on the children or young persons restrained.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such circumstances could add to the trauma faced by the children, and such actions seem an antithesis to the spirit of rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note and appreciate that this power is only sanctioned in very specific circumstances and, in practice, may be necessary.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that it is important for the Ministry to constantly assess the use of this provision and its impact on the children and young people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a need to review and strengthen the Act so that we can best address the needs of the sector and the community.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, some are beset with difficult circumstances which plague their early lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such youths will also be entitled to have their identities protected from publication throughout the proceedings and their lifetimes, to reduce the harm of stigmatisation and labelling which would jeopardise their futures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These changes will bring our laws in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which the Singapore Government ratified more than 20 years ago in 1995.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I have some specific observations and questions on the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are mainly about the fostering scheme, youth offenders, the new FGOs, and the right to be heard.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Where a child's parents are deemed incapable of caring for the child, the child may be placed in the care of a foster parent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This may be done with the consent of the parents under a voluntary care arrangement, or by an order of Court applied for by the Child Protective Service.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Volunteering to be a foster parent is an onerous responsibility, involving providing a home and caring for children whose backgrounds are difficult and who may exhibit challenging behaviours.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Sometimes, foster parents also face pressure from the child's natural parents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We must, indeed, thank the 500-over fostered parents who have signed up for this mission.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill strengthens the framework for fostering in a few ways.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, voluntary care arrangements are given statutory recognition in the proposed section 11A, which clarifies how these voluntary arrangements will be managed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the proposed section 27B, a Committee on Fostering will be set up to periodically review cases of children fostered out, to ascertain if the foster parent is implementing a proper care plan for the child.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, the Bill also gives more recognition to foster parents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, clause 63 will amend the Employment Act to enable the foster parent to take childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also note that under clause 69, an amendment is being made to the Passports Act to enable the Director-General, a protector or a foster parent to give consent for a child to be issued with a passport for international travel.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my opinion, this is a useful amendment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am aware of a case where the child's parent refused to give permission for the child to go to Malaysia with his foster family, as the parent was highly critical of the care given by the foster parent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was despite evidence that the child was happy and doing well in his foster home.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Once this amendment is made and under the ECPO, which the Minister just described, the child will no longer have to be left behind while his foster family went on holidays.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now come to a few issues concerning young persons who get into trouble with the criminal law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, I am quite concerned about clause 25 of the Bill which will amend section 30 of the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Section 30 currently provides that youths who are arrested and not released should be brought before the Youth Court or, if not possible, before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is an important safeguard to ensure that any further detention of young persons should be approved by a Court, and that the youth or his parents will have the opportunity to be heard before a Court before further detention is permitted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not know why there is a need to add in the words "within 48 hours", as this time limit is already provided under Article 9 of the Constitution and applies to all arrested persons, adult and young alike.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What concerns me is not the redundancy of the addition, but that law enforcement officers may take the addition of the 48-hour limit in the CYPA to wrongly assume that there is no additional urgency when dealing with young suspects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A child or young person in a Police lock-up, away from familiar surroundings, is vulnerable and needs to be processed fast.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I would like to ask whether our law enforcement officers have protocols that require them to process cases involving youth offenders at a faster pace, what shorter time limits are set out in these protocols and how these protocols are enforced.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On a related note, I would like to know if there is any special training being given to the law enforcement officers in handling suspects who are children or young persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a welcome move but, at the same time, significant limits have been placed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At first glance, I do appreciate that the offences listed at the new Second Schedule appear to be more serious, such as drug trafficking, robbery and certain moneylending-related offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would appear, however, that a youth who has a prior conviction of any offence, however minor, may also be tried in an adult Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 27 provides that in such situations, the Youth Court or the Public Prosecutor can initiate the transfer of the case from the Youth Court to the adult Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, I believe the Minister did touch on this point.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further, if the case gets transferred to an adult Court, which sits in public, how will the protection from publicising the youth's identity be enforced?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, I would like to ask about clause 32 which touches on Reformative Training (RT).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: RT is a tough regime that emphasises military-style discipline and involves participants who are older.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With these amendments, RT will usually be ordered for offenders between 18 and 21 years of age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the existing Act, section 44 provides that RT can only be imposed upon a young person below the usual age of RT under two situations: the first is that he had been sent to a JRC, that is, he has been sent to a JRC for an earlier offence and is now before the Court again, indicating that he might need a tougher Court order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second situation is that while the youth is serving detention in a JRC, the person in charge of the centre finds him so unruly that continued detention there is not feasible and RT may be needed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The wording of the proposed section 44(1)(k)(iii) is that an offender aged between 14 and 18 could be sent to RT if the Youth Court "is of the opinion that the offender is of so unruly a character that the offender cannot be safely detained in a JRC or a place of detention".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister earlier clarified in his speech that this will enable the Youth Court to send a youth to reformative training at the first instance even if he has never stayed at a JRC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On what basis then will the Youth Court conclude that he would be a failure at the JRC if he has never been sent there?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of the advantages of the Youth Court is its focus on formulating orders that are appropriate to each youth, depending on the Court's assessment of what is required in individual circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This advantage can also become a bone of contention, as several youths involved in the same incident may end up being treated differently by the Youth Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, a group of secondary school students who decide to steal motorcycles for a joy ride could end up getting different sentences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One could be ordered to undergo probation, where he continues his normal schooling and resides at home, subject to curfew hours; his accomplice, on the other hand, could be ordered to be detained in a JRC like the Singapore Boys Home, separated from his home environment, with normal schooling disrupted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such disparate treatment needs to be rigorously justified.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I remember years ago when I was representing a youth before the former Juvenile Courts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: His mother asked me point blank whether her son was ordered to be incarcerated because she was a divorcee, while his accomplice got a probation because he came from a two-parent household.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While certainly the Youth Court has to assess risk factors, I would caution that the system must never become so rigid as to underestimate the effort and resilience of persons facing challenges in life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the existing Act, parents who believe they are not able to manage their children can apply to Court to place them in the care of an institution or other person, under what is currently known as the BPC regime.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note that under clause 43, a Court making an GO may attach further orders for parents or the child to comply with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such orders include attending mediation, counselling, psychotherapy, assessments or other programmes or treatment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will parents be penalised if they are unable to pay the fees required to comply or will financial support be provided?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wish to raise a concern regarding the right to be heard before the Youth Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are various provisions in this Bill and in the Act itself that provide that before the Court makes an order, the child, young person or parent has the right to be heard.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, there is a right to be heard before care arrangements for a child are changed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is also a right to be heard when young offenders are about to be sentenced.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In theory, these persons have a right to engage a lawyer, but only a minority can afford one.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To represent oneself before a Court is unfamiliar to most people and I have observed that unrepresented persons tend to either not speak up or do the opposite by being argumentative and casting aspersions on Government officials, which will be most unhelpful to their causes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another typical problem is that what is said is not logically arranged and is difficult for the Court to follow.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I recently encountered a family who expressed frustration at their perception that the Court was not listening to them on the care arrangements for their son.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Upon probing further, I realised that the Court was not to be blamed but it was simply a matter of the parents organising their thoughts on paper and being respectful to the Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How can we facilitate the right to be heard, especially by the lower income?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Can there be more pro bono services available for family and youth matters?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure this sentiment is shared by other hon Members, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And the number of neglect cases has somewhat stayed in the 300 range since 2016.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is also troubling to see there is a rise in cases of kids between 13 and 15 years who are BPC.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our young not only can access all sorts of disturbing materials online, but are also basing their relationships and self-worth on social media.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They receive a lot of information, but might not be sufficiently mature to understand consequences.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What I would like to ask the Minister is what is there now, or anything in the pipeline, which helps the community to intervene, even before the kids reach this situation?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need parents who have difficulty handling their kids to be able to turn to someone for advice, counselling or guidance before the situation gets out of hand.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, they are so stressed out and they do not know how to handle their children and end up harming their children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Under what circumstances would they recommend to the Police to take action against a parent?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I raise this question because I want to share with the House an anecdote that happened where one of the parents, the father, was charged and jailed for beating the 10-year-old child.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This case went to Court and the father was jailed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But in the one year, between the time of offence to the Court sentence, the father and child had a very close relationship, going out together, bonding together.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, my question is what do counsellors and the Police take into consideration when recommending the offender for Court action?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think there are circumstances which merit consideration as, even today, the child and the offending parent are very close.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To me, the main thing is to look at how we can help to reconcile the child with the parent.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The offender can be warned, sent for counselling and so on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to ask, in the case of those children who are the subject of any investigation, how would the Ministry work with MOE so that the teacher would be able to pay special attention to the child, in case he or she needs extra care, or the teacher may need to be more sensitive to the trauma that the child might have gone through?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is to ensure that at least a family representative has a role in the whole process.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   I have heard of one case.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A father beat up his 10-year-old son but his relationship with the boy was still very close afterwards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the end, the father was sentenced to jail and was forced to be separated from the child.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I feel that parent-child relationship is a lifelong one.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When dealing with such cases, we should value the parent-child relationship more and be flexible in terms of punishment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also feel that when a child is abused or has behavioural issues, the Government should work together with the school to pay attention to the child's mental state.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the parents are not suitable to look after the child, should the designated caregiver consult the child's close relatives, such as grandparents, when making important decisions?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, there is an increasing number of cases of children being sexually abused or children beyond parental control.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before going into my points proper on the Bill, I would like to put on record my thanks to the hardworking and committed MSF officers who give of themselves in their calling, their duty to serve and protect among the most vulnerable in our society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Among last year's investigations, about half were physical abuse cases while about 20% involved sexual abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Remember, these abuse cases involve a family member.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not just statistics, these numbers reflect the number of young lives affected by domestic abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Children put into perspective the importance of CYPA which this Bill amends.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, how the Bill extends the applicability of CYPA; two, how youths are treated in the criminal justice system; three, how the Bill provides greater support for caregivers; and four, how the Bill provides greater discretion to MSF officers as to determining at points of intervention.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This brings it in line with some other statutes, such as the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act, which draws the line between adult and child protection at 18 years of age.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides amending the definition for young person to include those 18 and under, child trafficking offences in CYPA are extended from just children to include young persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 10 amends the heading for sections 12 to 18 so that the trafficking offences apply to children and young persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The words of the offences have similarly been expanded.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, section 12 prohibiting the transfer of possession, custody or control of a child for valuable consideration has been amended by clause 11, extending it to young persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Where the offence is under CYPA, the new section 84B ensures that the victim's identity is held in strict confidence even after the victim turns 18.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It may seem a slight amendment but actually has major positive consequences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The judge is also able to order takedown of publications in media as well as on social media.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Exceptions are at the Court's discretion in the interest of justice, as stated in the new section 84B(2).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Director-General and protector have stronger powers of investigation in the new section 8.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, although self-incriminating information cannot be withheld, they are inadmissible unless false information is provided.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As it is difficult for victims to retell the horrendous stories of abuse, would the Minister, therefore, provide an update on what is being done to minimise the trauma involved in recounting the harrowing experience, especially in Court settings?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Several changes to CYPA also better support the youth offender's rehabilitation and now reintegration into society, trying as best as possible that the past does not hold them back from achieving their potential and that they can continue to have hope for their future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One way is to allow sentences meted out by the Youth Court to be deemed as spent at the end of completing the supervision, detention, community sentence or fine, without needing to wait the normal three or so years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is provided for in clause 73 and allows youth offenders to more easily reintegrate into society as they can declare that they have no criminal record.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This enables the youth offender to turn over a new leaf.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, it creates a supporting scaffold structure around the youths, such as to be able to turn over a new leaf.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another way is by the extension of CYPA to those 18 and under and not just those 16 and below.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This provides young offenders access to a criminal justice system which places emphasis on rehabilitation and reintegration so that the mistakes of the past do not continue to haunt the young person when he or she is older.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One way is by providing for the youth offender's identity to be kept confidential for life and not just while he is still a young person, unless he or she reoffends.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This allows the young person's space to grow and change without being shackled to his past.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another example, and a good example, is clause 27(a) read with the Second Schedule within the Bill, which allows for the Prosecution or the Court to transmit cases involving the causing of grievous hurt, certain Misuse of Drugs Offences and other more serious offences to the Court of appropriate jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important for the Misuse of Drugs Act offences as we do not want our young persons to become targets for drug syndicates to hire them or manipulate them as mules just because they are specially treated by our criminal justice system or the Youth Courts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, this Bill provides greater support for those who care for children and young persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, I want to highlight the support that this Bill strives towards fostering.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 57 extends childcare leave to include foster children and allows the foster parent to disclose information necessary for this purpose.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is good that foster parents are supported in taking care of the children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They need the same kind of leave to be present for their children, for instance, if the child is sick or at a parent-teachers meeting.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They also need it in order to better ease a foster child into the family and bring the child for therapy sessions if therapy is necessary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By better supporting foster parents, hopefully more loving families will be willing to step up and provide a loving and caring environment for children and young persons, showing the foster child what family and parents' love look like.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, thereafter, hopefully, the child can be adopted either by the foster parents or parents who are hoping to adopt a child.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or if there can be reconciliation with the child's biological parents and the fostered child, then, if possible, the child can be reunited with the family, provided it is, indeed, safe.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On one hand, the protection of the child and, hence, the child's welfare and best interests are at risk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the other hand, the benefit of being cared for by his or her parent or guardian is significant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As mentioned in the beginning of my speech, the number of child abuse cases is concerning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When a child is abused, a child's life is at stake – not just physical but also the long-lasting emotional trauma from being emotionally or psychologically abused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a basic ingredient that I am supportive of.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The broader discretion through this Bill allows the Child Protection Service officers to make the necessary judgement as to when that intervention is necessary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With regard to the amended section 4(2) which sets out specific examples of emotional or psychological abuse, I do have a few clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Paragraph (a) mentions well-being and a sense of self-worth.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Paragraph (b) mentions that threatening to physically hurt the child or young person is child abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will the Minister clarify how this provision is to be understood in the context of section 64 of the Women's Charter where correction is an exception to "family violence"?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Paragraph (d) says that confining a child or young person to a small space for the purposes of discipline is considered abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on what is intended by the phrase "any small space"?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Paragraph (e) talks about influencing the development of self-destructive, criminal, deviant or other mal-adaptive behaviour.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the good Minister explain what is meant by "influence", "deviant" and "anti-social" behaviour?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, would the Minister explain what "infantilising" means in illustration (b)?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications above, Mr Speaker, Sir, it is important that enough latitude and discretion be given to Child Protection Service officers for swift intervention where necessary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister explain also the process of investigating a possible child abuse case and elaborate on the thoughts that go towards deciding how a child abuse case is best managed?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, under what circumstances will a child be removed from his or her parents, and, if that happens, will the child still have the opportunity to meet and even reconcile with his or her parents under appropriate circumstances?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This amendment broadens the discretion of the Child Protection Service officers and allows them to intervene swiftly where necessary.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is disturbing, especially given the psychological risks and effects of the use of physical restraints.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I believe this is already an MSF requirement for all children's homes, in keeping with the Standards of Care for Children and Young Persons Homes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Also, I understand that one out of three care staff has also been sent for the Management of Actual or Potential Aggression (MAPA®) training programme to ensure that personnel involved in handling crisis situations can maintain the care, welfare, safety and security of all involved.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I am not sure if I understand the intent and need for section 68A.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Parents and guardians are expected to exercise responsibility for their children, but I would argue if families are adequately enabled and empowered.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because we all know that there are many ways in which a family situation may manifest itself, depending on the parenting attitudes as well as who are the present and absent family members, their dynamics, needs and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Take Farhana, 47, and a single mother living in Yio Chu Kang who used to struggle with raising her five children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She barely had time for herself with taking care of the children and trying to earn some money from home, so she often felt exhausted trying to hold it all together.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At times, she also resorted to physical methods with her children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When her eldest child was not attending school regularly, the state intervened and later found out about the abuse.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She was then required to attend counselling and therapy sessions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Ironically, the well-meaning sessions which were meant to help her and her children saw her in even more emotional distress, which clearly also affected the psychological well-being of her children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the support for Farhana should have come earlier?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Family Service Centres, when working with families, could suggest counselling or parenting courses if the staff are also trained to assess parenting capacity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to parents, when a child or young person is in a care placement outside the family, whether short or long term, retention of relationships with the extended family or significant people, like grandparents and siblings, is critical for their sense of identity to be preserved, unless it is contrary to the best interest of the child.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The UN Guidelines for the Alternative Care of Children states that it is important to keep siblings together in any alternative care placements.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When siblings are separated, it causes anxiety among them, with separated siblings often having to manage lifelong issues of attachment, identity and loss in their lives.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I know that Darul Ihsan Orphanages is one of the residential home facilities that provide care for both girls and boys with deliberate joint activities to facilitate sibling interaction.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are nearly 10 sibling group placements within the home of 50 children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, we should extend family work intervention to the other sibling who is in the household to prevent further family separation and risk being referred to the care system in the future, too.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The demand for foster parents is more pressing now, as more children have entered the foster care system in recent years.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A children's home, no matter how well-run, cannot replicate the "therapeutic elements" found in a family, said Dr Yong Ming Lee of the National Institute of Education.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, we could reframe foster care to also include kinship care and incentivise keeping children within their families by extending the amendments to section 27C to enable grandparents and next-of-kin, such as uncles and aunts, to childcare leave and unpaid infant care leave.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Hong Kong had piloted a two-year project on Child Care Training for Grandparents with the aim to strengthen inter-generational family ties as well as scaling up childcaring skills.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Perhaps we can learn from such initiatives as we align family policies with Active Ageing in strengthening family bonds.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The amount a foster carer would receive then takes into account both the "placement type", for example, care for children with special needs and disabilities alongside their "competence" to provide care for the children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: This has been implemented in many independent, for-profit agencies, charities and area councils in the UK.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: And, finally, Mr Speaker, let us go upstream to look at preventive measures.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Preventing delinquency and ongoing offending behaviours is as important as downstream interventions, if not more so, so that our children and youths can avoid the harmful effects of detention and incarceration, and the potential involvement with the adult criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: One of the risk factors for delinquency is mental health disorders, which is increasing amongst children and young persons in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: A global study showed that young persons diagnosed with major depressive disorder were found to be more vulnerable to involvement in violence.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: It also found that depression in children and young persons may be harder to recognise and could manifest itself as irritability and aggressiveness.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: There is accumulating evidence that depression can be predictors of youth delinquency.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Can we create an inclusive environment by training community workers to identify and respond to these mental health risk factors as well?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: How can we do more to provide our children and the young persons with a nurturing and stimulating environment, especially so in at-risk neighbourhoods?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Community workers at Beyond Social Services facilitate competent communities in rental housing neighbourhoods across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: They believe in engaging children and young persons in the longer term, and nurture family and community support around them.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: An example of a participatory design project is at the Kebun Baru neighbourhood where community needs assessment conducted earlier in the year highlighted the needs of the children and young persons, such as the lack of playground, halal food facilities and the feeling of a safe, inclusive environment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Currently, community-based conversations are being held with grassroots support to visualise what different segments of the community would envision for their neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Another example of repurposing the immediate environment is Project Hearts in Nee Soon East which also highlights active citizenry among its residents.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The group saw a need to kick off with academic and play support programmes for the children in Yishun Blocks 269A and 269B.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Bernard, born with a congenital development condition that affects the spine, leads the academic outreach of Project Hearts in collaboration with the Singapore Red Cross.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: During the sessions, the void deck is converted into a study area with portable chairs and tables, and the session caters to the needs of children in the area.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The children feel they are part of a community whilst their academic and play needs are being met in a holistic way.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: It takes a community to raise a child, indeed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: How can we enable more of such efforts that empower the community and, therefore, our children and youths?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Children and youths are key drivers for inclusive growth and sustainable development of a society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Because it is easier to build strong children than to repair broken men and women.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We – the Government, the community and the family – must share this paramount responsibility of protecting each and every one of our children and young persons and do everything possible to create enabling and nurturing environments for them to learn, live, love and be loved so that they can thrive and contribute meaningfully to society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Before I completely end, I would like to also take this opportunity, Mr Speaker, to thank the everyday and invisible heroes in child protection work from the Ministry and the community for their dedication and compassion.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I stand in staunch support of the Children and Young Persons (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I especially welcome the provisions to further protect the identity of the child.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As it stands, the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA) restricts the publication and broadcast of any information relating to Court proceedings involving children and young people aged 16 and below that reveals their names, images, addresses, schools or other particulars.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In so doing, we can, therefore, insulate our young people a little longer from media coverage of their offences and our efforts to rehabilitate and reintegrate them will be far more effective.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Research from the United States (US) shows that media coverage of juvenile offences that fails to protect the identities of young offenders can have various detrimental consequences.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: First, the public shaming of young offenders can heighten tensions within their families and fracture the very unit of society that can play a pivotal role in these youths’ rehabilitation.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Second, media coverage can lead these youths to be ostracised by their peers and teachers, thus crippling community-based rehabilitation measures.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Third, negative media coverage can also lend offenders a semblance of celebrity status.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In an era where it seems to be cool to go viral whatever the reason, media coverage of juvenile offences may encourage the tendency to re-offend and, possibly, influence other youths to commit similar crimes to attain notoriety and peer affirmation.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, my own research on the social media practices of juvenile offenders in Singapore reveals an interest among some youths to project a cool and tough image online by boasting of their misdemeanours on social media.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: One boy in my study had even shared a newspaper report of his crime on his social media accounts until his social worker cautioned him that it was very foolish to do so.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, given the replicability and durability of online images and reports, it is extremely difficult to “rewrite” one’s personal history.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Extending identity protection to the age of 18 is, therefore, a timely and enlightened move, given that our public identities assume an oversized importance in our digitally-connected society as we concluded in our debate on the Protection from Online Harassment Act in May.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With two additional years of confidentiality for young offenders, we can derive considerable social and developmental returns in our Internet-saturated society.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, given our society’s growing technologisation, I would like to take this opportunity to raise the issue of the digital rights of children.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: At first blush, you may find it laughable to speak about digital rights for young people in Singapore since, wherever we turn, it seems like every toddler, teen and young adult seems to be attached to a digital device of their own.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: What is of urgent import is that children be accorded rights to the necessary protections in a rapidly and ferociously digitalising world.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: By that, I refer to how young people are increasingly the target of commercial exploitation in the online world.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Principally, our society needs to ensure that children enjoy rights to privacy and not have their data harvested and mined for profit.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The same Google survey found that teachers here are more worried than parents about cyberbullying, while parents are most concerned about their children’s privacy and security online.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Children’s privacy and security online are, indeed, a matter that requires closer attention.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Take the example of the Internet of Toys.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Children use the company's Kids Connect app in conjunction with these electronic toys.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Through this app, VTech collected a vast trove of information, including children’s names, contact information, photographs and audio files, without seeking consent from parents or even informing them.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: A security breach revealed that the company had failed to secure their young users’ data, allowing hackers untrammelled access.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Companies must also be urged to present their terms and conditions in a far more child-friendly and accessible manner so that young people know what they are signing up for when they use online services.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Even for companies that do have adequate data protection measures, we must consider how such data is used to develop algorithms to create or serve up more content targeted at children.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Gaming, online shopping, content sharing and social media platforms profit significantly from the digital native market.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: However, the companies behind them often fail to take into account the responsibilities they have towards these young users and simply find more ways to engage them, for longer periods and with ever more alluring content that resonates with their interests.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Young people then find themselves irresistibly drawn to these platforms, often using their digital devices excessively.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The burden is then shifted to schools and parents who must persuade or even coerce young people to better manage their use of digital media.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In such a climate, we must exhort technology companies to do more to create a safe and edifying digital environment for young people.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This meeting arose in part from the suicide of 14-year-old British teenager Molly Russell.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Her family believed she took her own life because her Instagram account was replete with material about depression, self-harm and suicide.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: So, young Singaporeans' exposure to such content and their effects should also be more closely investigated.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: When our children go online, they are, indeed, vulnerable to risks – risks of commercial exploitation, exposure to inappropriate content, cyberbullying and online sexual abuse, and we must do our best to shield them from these dangers.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
